text: At the time, we didn't really have a solid product yet. We would have 10 to 15 meetings every day with potential customers. I was hired as the first product manager. I sat in on those calls.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks Raaz about the early days at Wiz when the company was struggling to find the right product direction. Raaz explains how she joined as the first product manager during a confusing period where the team was having many customer meetings but nobody really understood what they were building. After weeks of customer calls where she couldn't grasp what product they were supposed to develop, she finally asked the direct question that led to their successful pivot to cloud security.
text_ko: 그때는 아직 확실한 제품이 없었어요. 잠재 고객들과 하루에 열에서 열다섯 번씩 미팅을 했고, 저는 첫 번째 제품 관리자(product manager)로 채용돼서 그 통화들에 직접 참여했어요.
text_zh: 那时候我们的产品还不够成熟。我们每天要跟潜在客户开十到十五场会。我是第一个被招来的产品经理(product manager)，那些电话/会议我都会参加。
text_es: Por entonces todavía no teníamos un producto sólido. Teníamos entre 10 y 15 reuniones al día con clientes potenciales. Me contrataron como el primer responsable de producto (product manager). Me unía a esas llamadas.
key_sentence: I was hired as the first product manager.
original_text: At the time, we didn't really have a solid product yet. We would have 10 to 15 meetings every day with potential customers. I was hired as the first product manager. I sat in on those calls. I still did not exactly understand what we were going to build, which was confusing, because I was a product manager, so I was supposed to start building it, and so, at some point, it was like, "I have to ask, what exactly are we doing here?" And that ended up pivoting us around to cloud security.

vocabulary.definition: A product manager is a professional responsible for the strategy, roadmap, and feature definition of a product or product line. They act as a liaison between various departments to ensure the product meets market needs and business goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, product managers play a crucial role in guiding the development process and aligning the product with customer expectations and company objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a blend of technical knowledge, business acumen, and leadership skills, making it a multifaceted role that can vary significantly between organizations.

vocabulary.definition: Potential customers are individuals or organizations that have the capacity to purchase a product or service but have not yet made a purchase. They represent a target market segment that businesses aim to convert into actual customers.
vocabulary.businessContext: Identifying and engaging with potential customers is vital for businesses, especially startups, as it helps in validating product ideas and refining marketing strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term suggests an opportunity for growth and sales, and it is often used in discussions about market research and customer acquisition strategies.

vocabulary.definition: A solid product refers to a well-developed, reliable, and effective offering that meets customer needs and expectations. It is characterized by quality, functionality, and user satisfaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and product development, having a solid product is essential for attracting customers, securing funding, and achieving market success.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase conveys a sense of confidence and assurance in the product's value, often used to differentiate between a prototype and a market-ready offering.

text: We really felt the type of questions change, right? Silly.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about the signals that showed when Wiz finally found product-market fit after their pivot to cloud security. Raaz describes how customer conversations completely changed from polite interest to urgent practical questions. She explains that customers stopped saying generic positive things and started asking specific questions about pricing and proof-of-value (POV) trials, indicating real purchasing intent rather than just politeness.
text_ko: 질문 유형이 확실히 달라진 걸 정말 체감했죠? 좀 어이없었어요.
text_zh: 我们明显感觉到问的问题类型变了，对吧？有点可笑。
text_es: De verdad notamos que cambió el tipo de preguntas, ¿no? Qué tontería.
key_sentence: We really felt the type of questions change.
original_text: We really felt the type of questions change, right? Silly. The call sounded like, again, "How are you pricing this, or when can we start doing a POV?" I think naturally, as human beings, you have a bias to look for affirmation, versus a bias for what you don't want to hear.

text: I had a ton to learn about marketing, with what I knew really well, with the problem we solved, and I really knew our audience.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks why Raaz thinks she was successful in marketing despite being new to the field. Raaz explains her unconventional approach to becoming CMO at Wiz. While she had no traditional marketing experience, she had deep domain expertise in cloud security and understood the target audience intimately because she lived in that space as a former customer herself.
text_ko: 마케팅(marketing)에 대해 배울 게 정말 많았어요. 다만 제가 확실히 알고 있던 건 우리가 해결한 문제와 우리 대상 고객(audience)이었어요.
text_zh: 虽然我对我们做的事、要解决的问题和目标用户都很清楚，但在市场营销(marketing)这块我还有很多要学的。
text_es: Tenía muchísimo que aprender sobre mercadotecnia (marketing), aunque conocía muy bien el problema que resolvíamos y sabía quién era nuestra audiencia.
key_sentence: I had a ton to learn about marketing in my space.
original_text: I had a ton to learn about marketing, with what I knew really well, with the problem we solved, and I really knew our audience. I myself, I come from security, I come from cloud security, I read all of the right Twitters, and I follow all of the right people on Twitter, and I read all of the right blogs. I know it's funny, I know what matters, I know it's interesting right now, generally because, this is my space.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who are targeted for communication, marketing, or information dissemination.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding the audience is crucial for tailoring marketing strategies and ensuring that products or services meet the needs and preferences of potential customers.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'audience' often refers to consumers, it can also apply to stakeholders, investors, or any group that may influence or be influenced by a business's activities.

text: Marketing is quite the opposite, in my opinion. There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about Raaz's approach to creating noise and taking risks in marketing. Raaz contrasts marketing with product development, explaining how product features require careful consideration because they consume engineering resources and create permanent complexity. She describes marketing's advantage of being able to experiment freely without long-term consequences, allowing for rapid testing and iteration.
text_ko: 제 생각엔 마케팅은 완전히 반대예요. 비용도 들지 않고, 유지보수(maintenance)도 필요 없고, 기술적 깊이(technical depth)도 없고, 아무것도 없어요.
text_zh: 我觉得营销（marketing）恰恰相反：好像什么都不用花成本、也不用维护、没什么技术含量，基本上什么都不需要。
text_es: El marketing, para mí, es justo lo contrario: no implica coste alguno, no necesita mantenimiento, no requiere profundidad técnica (technical depth)… vamos, que no exige nada.
key_sentence: There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything.
original_text: Marketing is quite the opposite, in my opinion. There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything. If tomorrow I post a video on Wiz's LinkedIn page, and I think that video is super funny, and nobody likes that video, nothing happened. Tomorrow, I'll post a different video, no maintenance, bye-bye, forgot it ever happened.

vocabulary.definition: The extent of knowledge and expertise in a specific technical area, often involving complex concepts and advanced skills.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'technical depth' is crucial for developing innovative products and solutions, as it indicates the team's ability to handle intricate challenges and leverage advanced technologies.
vocabulary.nuance: This term is often used to emphasize the importance of specialized knowledge in fields like engineering or software development, and may imply that a lack of technical depth can lead to superficial solutions.

text: Almost every single thing I've done in my career, in some ways, even before, I never thought I was going to be successful in it. I guess there's a lot of times, it's a lot of talk about being more confident than yourself.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks Raaz about her mindset regarding failure and risk-taking throughout her career. Raaz shares her contrarian approach to confidence and imposter syndrome. Rather than trying to build false confidence, she embraces the expectation of failure while still taking on challenging opportunities. She explains how this mindset actually liberates her to take bigger risks and attempt things outside her comfort zone.
text_ko: 제 커리어에서 해온 거의 모든 일들, 심지어 그 전에 했던 일들도 마찬가지로, 그게 성공할 거라고 생각해본 적이 거의 없어요. 아마도 많은 경우에 실제로 느끼는 자신감보다 더 자신감 있는 척하라는 얘기가 많더라고요.
text_zh: 回头看我职业生涯里几乎做过的每件事，甚至更早之前，我都没想过自己会成功。我觉得很多时候，不过是自我鼓劲，让自己看起来比实际更有自信。
text_es: En casi todo lo que he hecho en mi carrera, incluso antes, nunca pensé que tendría éxito. Supongo que muchas veces se trata de actuar con más seguridad de la que realmente sientes.
key_sentence: I never thought I was going to be successful in it.
original_text: Almost every single thing I've done in my career, in some ways, even before, I never thought I was going to be successful in it. I guess there's a lot of times, it's a lot of talk about being more confident than yourself. I don't know, at least for me, I don't really know if that's a real option, okay? I just know that I'm kind of okay with being pretty sure I'm going to fail at something, and still attempting it.

text: Every time you write something, I wanted to not assume knowledge about Wiz, or knowledge about the product, or deep knowledge about the market. I'll give just a simple example.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about Raaz's concept of the 'dummy explanation' and how to avoid assuming too much knowledge in marketing communications. Raaz explains her philosophy of avoiding insider jargon and technical terminology that only people within the company would understand. She gives a specific example of how even mentioning their own 'Wiz Graph Database' assumes knowledge that external audiences wouldn't have, emphasizing the need to communicate in universally understandable terms.
text_ko: 글을 쓸 때마다 저는 Wiz에 대해 알고 있다는 전제나 제품에 대한 이해, 또는 시장에 대해 깊게 알고 있다는 가정을 하고 싶지 않았어요. 간단한 예를 하나 들게요.
text_zh: 每次你写东西，我都希望你别默认读者知道Wiz（Wiz）、这个产品，或对市场有很深的认识。我就举个简单的例子。
text_es: Cada vez que escribes algo, procuro no dar por sentado que quien lo lea conozca Wiz, el producto o el mercado a fondo. Te doy un ejemplo sencillo.
key_sentence: Don't assume knowledge about Wiz or its deep innovation.
original_text: Every time you write something, I wanted to not assume knowledge about Wiz, or knowledge about the product, or deep knowledge about the market. I'll give just a simple example. Wiz itself is based on, part of the deep innovation that Wiz brought to the market that enabled the scale, was a very high correlated signal that's based on a graph database. So inside Wiz, we have the Wiz graph database, for security. If you write something that says, the Wiz Graph Database, I don't like it. Because why would a common person know it is the Wiz Graph Database, right?

vocabulary.definition: To take for granted or accept something as true without proof or verification.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, assuming can lead to miscommunication or misalignment if team members do not share the same understanding of a project or concept.
vocabulary.nuance: While assuming can streamline decision-making, it is often better to verify information to avoid potential pitfalls.

vocabulary.definition: The information, understanding, or skills acquired through experience or education.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, knowledge is critical for informed decision-making, strategy development, and competitive advantage.
vocabulary.nuance: Knowledge can be both explicit, such as documented information, and tacit, which is more intuitive and experience-based.
